item.title: Profiling Neovim on big logs: a growing 87 MB log froze the UI 11 s out of every 15
item.author: william
item.description:
After the startup pass, the slowest thing left in my Neovim was big log files. ~/log holds logs from 0.5 MB to 136 MB. The one I read most is 87 MB: 176,939 lines of about 500 characters, growing by about 2 lines a second while I read it. Opening it took 1.9 s before Neovim accepted a key. n, /, typing and <Esc> each stalled. Just reading the log while it grew froze the UI for about 11 of every 15 seconds.

No single plugin was to blame. Several separate pieces of work grew with the file, and one key mapping slowed n in every file. Medians of 5 runs in a real terminal:

before after
open the 87 MB log until keys are accepted 1857 ms 199 ms
n 523 ms 21 ms
UI blocked per 15 s while reading the growing log 10963 ms 0 ms

item.title: Profiling Neovim startup: lazy-loaded plugins that weren't lazy
item.author: william
item.description:
Update 2026-10-17: the next pass looked at big log files, and found an nc mapping that made every n wait timeoutlen (500 ms) in every file. See Profiling Neovim on big logs.

After tmux and zsh, I looked at Neovim. My config has grown to 138 plugins on lazy.nvim and LazyVim. Almost every spec has an event, cmd or keys, so I assumed most of them were lazy. They weren’t: 89 of the 138 plugins loaded at startup.

None of the causes was a slow plugin. They were config mistakes that only show up once you ask lazy.nvim why each plugin loaded. I fixed them in two rounds:

before after
CPU time to first screen, opening a new file ~150 ms ~120 ms
CPU time to first screen, no file (dashboard) 69 ms 50 ms
plugins loaded at startup 89 73

item.title: Profiling zsh: a Python plugin was adding 190 ms to every command
item.author: william
item.description:
After fixing tmux, I looked at the shell running inside it. My zsh config had grown over a few years to about 30 plugins and Oh My Zsh snippets on top of zinit and Powerlevel10k. It felt a little heavy, but nothing stood out.

Measured properly, it was slow in three separate ways, each with its own cause:

before after
startup to a usable shell 267 ms 101 ms
added to every command 188 ms 3 ms
added to every prompt 15 ms 4 ms

This post covers how I measured each one, the fixes, and how I checked that the fixes didn’t change anything else. That check caught two mistakes of my own.

item.title: Why my tmux was laggy: the status bar was forking a 1.2 GB server 24 times a second
item.author: william
item.description:
Update 2026-10-02: two days later the lag was back. Each fork of the server had become slow (~30 ms), and one claim below was wrong: passing #{E:#{@quote_cond}} into the job does not work, because tmux does not apply strftime inside a #() command. See round 2.

My tmux had started to feel sluggish. Nothing was broken, it just felt heavy. It turned out the tmux server was using about a third of a CPU core all the time, and nearly all of that went on the status bar. Part of the cost came from the clock workaround in my previous post.

This post covers how I tracked it down, including two wrong guesses, and the fix, which brought the server from ~35% CPU to ~4% without restarting it.
